name: Leo’s House of Thirst
review: Bubbles for breakfast, wine for lunch, aperitifs in the afternoon, and coffees from open to close are all in the house at Leo’s House of Thirst since owner Drew Wallace and partner-chef Austin Inselman expanded service hours and growth spurted the menu. Leo’s made its debut from a small, renovated cinderblock building in West Asheville in 2020 with an emphasis on wine and outdoor evening dining in response to COVID. Five years in, Wallace revived his original concept of a menu that seamlessly but distinctly segues from breakfast sandwiches, toasts, short rib hash, and Belgian waffles to soup, salad, shrimp rolls, and grilled cheese, to an hour-long snacky/small plates afternoon intermezzo, then finishes strong with Leo’s greatest dinner hits of pastas and roast chicken. Don’t pass on the baked goods or seasonal desserts.

name: Finest
review: When Boston native Mike Bean launched his sandwich pop-up under the Finest banner at the weekly West Asheville tailgate market in 2023, the enthusiastic feedback urged him to open a brick-and-mortar. There just happened to be an available address a couple blocks away, and after an extensive renovation — and some key additions to the team — Finest opened for breakfast, lunch, and all-day brunch, supported by a beverage program built by fellow New Yorker, co-owner, and certified cicerone Gab Bonfiglio.

name: Rowan Coffee
review: It took a coffee roaster and a designer to fully realize the aesthetic and business potential of a former auto garage in West Asheville. Bow Smith, who opened the first Rowan Coffee in a historic building in downtown Asheville, had long pined for space, but it wasn’t until he toured it for the first time that he realized there was room to fulfill his ultimate dream of a roastery and cafe under one roof. He got to work and turned the gorgeous bones of brick, banks of multi-paned original glass windows, polished concrete floors, and high ceilings over to his wife, Jessi Lee Cord. Neighborhood residents and friends fill the bar, banquettes, vintage leather booths, and covered outdoor seating for their fill of coffee drinks, wine, beer, baked goods, snacks, apps, pop-up chef dinners, and intermittent oyster nights.

name: Harmony Wine
review: Since opening Neng Jr. in West Asheville in 2022, married partners Silver and Cherry Iocovozzi have double-teamed the award-winning restaurant where Silver is the chef, and Cherry is the wine director. With the opening of Harmony Wine, a natural wine bar/bottle shop/listening room/reading nook up a couple of stairs in a sexy secret space in the same building, Cherry has his own little lair. Inspired by vintage photos of Silver’s mother at work in a Japanese karaoke bar, Shnozui and Meikyoku Kissa Lion Cafe in Tokyo, Ruby in San Francisco and Pompette in Copenhagen, Harmony is outfitted with books, meaningful memorabilia, photographs, prints, posters and bottles and bottles of natural wine from France, Italy, Spain, Mexico, Chile, Austria, Germany, Japan, and the United States. All of the wine can be taken home or enjoyed at the four-stool bar or a table. While karaoke will break out from time to time, Harmony’s soundtrack comes from the couple’s CD collection, run through 1960s Fisher receivers and Bozak speakers. “Snacks” made in Neng’s kitchen have included duck rillettes with a muscadine jam and a beautiful pork pate seasoned with galangal, ginger, chile, jujubee, and pistachio.

name: Piccolina
review: Piccolina is dedicated to Italian sandwiches, Neapolitan-style pizza, and desserts. Piccolina means little one, which reflects the small slot of space within the Aura Arts Building, but is a big dream come unexpectedly true for Elana and Nathan Pearlman. The couple met at the CIA in Hyde Park. After graduating, they moved to Austin, where they married and built their careers, then left Texas behind to explore Charleston and Asheville. In the former, they stumbled upon Welton’s Tiny Bakeshop and influential owners Hannah and Zach Welton, taking a cue from their business model. In Asheville, they stumbled upon an available space with a hood, ordered a Neapolitan pizza oven, and built out 400 of the 800-square-foot room with 20 seats.

name: Crusco
review: Every new restaurant arrives with expectations, but for Crusco, which opened on July 30, the weight of those was especially heavy. It took over the space that housed the popular independent restaurant Vivian, which closed after Helene. It is located in the upper section of the River Arts District, which bore the brunt of the French Broad River’s impact. Most profoundly, the owners are the core team that worked for beloved chef Brian Canipelli at Cucina 24, Asheville’s most respected and authentic Italian restaurant. Canipelli’s sudden death on February 6 permanently closed Cucina and shattered the lives of his life partner, Kat Kearney, chefs Lauren Macellaro and Alex Harris, and beverage director Allen Clark. Crusco — named for a sweet red Italian pepper Canipelli was enamored with — is how the partners began to put those broken pieces back together.

name: Posana Biltmore Park
review: Since 2009, Posana restaurant has been a welcoming beacon for modern fine dining in downtown Asheville. All of the deliciousness — from bread service to pasta course to dessert — based on local, regional, and seasonal sourcing is cooked and baked in an entirely gluten-free kitchen. In October, Martha and Peter Pollay gifted restaurant-bereft Biltmore Town Park Square with a second location, in an equally stylish room and menu thoughtful of every diner. Expect signature OG Posana dishes like kale salad, house-made gnocchi, and cheddar biscuits, and evolving presentations of pasta, vegetables, and the highest quality proteins. Posana Biltmore Park has added lunch service Monday to Friday and weekend brunch (gluten-free bagels, French toast, biscuits, and doughnut holes).

name: Chorizo
review: Chef Hector Diaz has been feeding Ashevillians and tourists for over thirty years from a quartet of downtown, internationally-inspired restaurants: Salsas, Modesto, Bomba, and, until its closure in 2016, Chorizo. Ten years later, Chorizo is back with a focus on tapas and dishes from southern Spain, particularly Córdoba, Madrid, and Andalusia, and a beverage program of Spanish wines, sherry, vermouth, and fancy cocktails. A sunny yellow awning hangs over the entrance on the Page Avenue side of the historic Grove Arcade, marking the spot for breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

name: SEN Vietnamese Street Food
review: The minute guests walk into the shotgun space that opened in December, the intoxicating scent from the open kitchen set against one wall compels them to quickly claim one of the 45 seats. The decor is minimalist, the ambiance serene, the menu for now is succinct, but the local chatter around the new restaurant is at high velocity. Vietnamese-born chef Quyen Hawes is the heart and hands behind the pho, which comes with a choice of four proteins in a deeply flavored 15-hour broth. Her parents are the helping hands in the kitchen, and her husband, Jesse Hawes, can usually be found out front. House-made peanut sauce comes with fried egg rolls and fresh spring rolls. The Cơm tấm Sườn Nướng Ốp La — a grilled, marinated pork chop served with a runny-yolk fried egg, broken rice vermicelli, and house-made condiments — is getting raves. No alcoholic beverages yet, but Vietnamese coffee brings the buzz.

name: Day Trip
review: Post Helene, the Asheville hospitality industry has fortified itself with stories of silver linings; few shine as brightly as Day Trip cocktail lounge, which saw its original site on Amboy Road swept away by the French Broad River one month after opening. Not to be deterred, owners Brandon Davis and Davie Roberts picked themselves up, brushed off their leisure suits, and found a space four times bigger — and far, far away from a body of water. The married couple is all in on 70s decor, mined from thrift stores and estate sales; patrons can time travel through rooms decked out with the greatest hits of basement rec rooms, snazzy bachelor pads, Aunt Betty’s kitschy breakfast nook, and your grandma’s living room if she used her ironing board as a coffee table. It’s a fun spot for your cocktails, mocktails, wine, beer, and charcuterie boards from Asheville Charcuterie Co.

name: Periscope
review: Prosecco and pie? Sure. And you can at Periscope, the newest tenant in the S&W Market. Take a seat in the snazzy cocktail lounge on the mezzanine level and channel your inner F. Scott Fitzgerald characters with fast craft cocktails and natural wines created and selected by Becky Bronson and Spencer Schultz, well-known names in artisan beverage circles. Among cocktails on draft are the Negroni alla contrada with London dry gin, red bitter and vermouth di torino; Mexican vesper with agave spirit blend, cardamaro and ancho chili; and raspberry Americano with raspberry apertivo, rose vermouth, black pepper and soda. The pie comes from the Queen of Pie, Schultz’s sister-in-law, Ashley Capps, creator of the famous banana pudding pie while pastry chef at Buxton Hall Barbecue and co-owner with Travis Schultz of New Stock.

name: Easy Tiger
review: Easy Tiger aims to be the ultimate destination for sports enthusiasts. Just in time for weekends bursting with college and pro gridiron, MLB playoffs, NBA and NHL, it’s flipping on a dozen big-screen TVs, firing up the fryers, polishing the bar, and hooking up the kegs.

name: Xico
review: Xico (shee-ko) describes itself as a Cocino de Fuego and Marisqueria — cooking on fire and seafood. Named for a small village in Veracruz, Mexico, Xico has a big vision for its large space in the South Slope. Culinarily driven by serial restaurateur/chef Scott Lindquist, Xico fires up much of its menu in a custom-built Jospur charcoal oven and wood-fired grill, like the bone-in angus ribeye for two and whole butterfly snapper. Tortillas are made fresh from Mexican heirloom corn nixtamal, and Josper-charred Spanish octopus is served with Oaxacan green mole. Table-side Caesar preparation is a special touch, as is the Margarita Classico using the original 1938 recipe from Rancho la Gloria in Baja, California, where legend says the margarita was born.

name: Birdie’s Pizza
review: New York-style pizza can be the opening for a food fight among aficionados, particularly those from New York. Justin Balzer — who is not from NY — defines it as a ‘20-inch round, thin-crust, crispy bottom — the ultimate mobile food, but also a meal.” Christine Costa Balzer is most definitely from New York. “My grandparents came from Italy, my family is Sicilian, I was born in New York, and raised in Jersey. This is my culture. I know a good New York pizza.” After many years working on their dough — from an eight-year-old sourdough starter — and seeking a downtown location that would accommodate families dining in, around a table, or grabbing a slice to fold and go — the married chefs opened Birdie’s Pizza on July 13 on busy Biltmore Avenue. Choose from one of eight pies – round, Sicilian, or by the slice, made with hand-stretched mozzarella, organic tomatoes, and toppings like caramelized onion, roasted red pepper, spicy sausage, and crispy chicken cutlets. Wait for your pie to finish with garlic knots, arancini, meatballs, or cacio e pepe fries.

name: Baba Nahm
review: Fast, friendly service, casual indoor/outdoor seating, and thoughtfully adapted Middle Eastern street food — think pita wraps, build-your-own-bowls, dolmas, bourekas, and hummus — made Baba Nahm one of Asheville’s most frequent go-to lunch spots for downtown workers. Its popularity outgrew its tiny slice of the Grove Arcade, and chef-owners Laura and Brian Smith’s culinary ambition outgrew the rudimentary kitchen, so they found bigger digs on busy Biltmore Avenue, with a real dining room, a real bar, a real kitchen with a real hood, and expanded service hours to include breakfast and dinner. Lunch now includes kabobs, a lamb and beef pita burger, a crispy chicken schnitzel sandwich, and meal-sized salads. A succinct dinner menu of apps and entrees changes weekly. Cult favorite Baba fries — smothered in tomato jam, tahini, and harissa — are available from open to close.

name: Finch Grocery
review: Finch Grocery was one of dozens of businesses badly damaged or destroyed when the Swannanoa River swept through Biltmore Village post-Helene. In the twee-est of the twee historic pebbledash cottages in Biltmore Village, Finch was tucked into the alley behind Scout Boutique and stocked from floor to ceiling with wine, packaged gourmet foods, condiments, tea, coffee, chocolate, linens, entertainment accessories, and paper goods. In early 2024, new owners introduced made-to-order lunch items to coffee drinks, tea, and fresh pastries, and added an outdoor patio for seating. The good news is, in October, Finch moved from 10 ½ All Souls Crescent to 10 All Souls Crescent, taking over the Scout building, expanding their footprint, inventory, and menu (wine by the glass, beer, and cider also available). Don’t miss their famous lemon bars.

name: Zella’s Deli
review: Hot Buns and Tasty Meat were the magic words that drew diners to Zella’s Deli when it first opened on College Street in downtown Asheville in the spring of 2024. The restaurant drew on industry vets John Tressler and Mike Reppert’s urban, northeastern roots (Pittsburgh and New York, respectively) and built a menu based on sandwiches, sides, and salads inherent to the delis they grew up with. That includes Jewish deli classics like pastrami on rye, corned beef, lox and bagels, and branding two sandwiches with their names — Mikey’s meatball sub and Johnny’s Italian (capicola, salami, pepperoni, provolone, lettuce, and tomato. Don’t dare ask for mayo.)
